rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Custom board 2.1 Official rules 2.2 Unofficial alternative rules Overview The first player starts the game by placing a piece from their hand onto a square on the outer edge of the board. Players then take turns to place pieces in unoccupied spaces. Each piece dictates where your opponent must play next: Straights: same row or column Diagonals: in a diagonal line Pusher: not adjacent Puller: adjacent If there are no spaces where you can legally play, you must pass. Your opponent is now free to play in any empty space. Score a point for each line of three pieces of your colour. A line of four counts as two overlapping lines of three, so scores two points. The game ends when a player cannot play because they have no more pieces. Custom board Official rules Game gaps between squares of the board block Straights and Diagonals. Unofficial alternative rules Straights and diagonals permit placement across gaps in the board.

community_text:
[Rating: 3/10] Very dry and unexciting. Too short to develop any sort of flow, so strategy will be entirely determined by the first 2-3 moves. This turns it into more of a puzzle than a real game, with interest not brought in by the other player but by the varying board configuration. I suspect that between players who have played a dozen times each most of the time will be spent thinking about the empty board, then playing through.

[Rating: 4/10] An inoffensive and small abstract game. Nothing spectacular here, but fun to while away a short pause with. Would probably work best as a Clemens Gerhards production so that it becomes a good showpiece too; the current multiplex with laser-burnt symbols looks and feels very cheap. 1 point deduction because of this. Competitor Quarto! does more or less the same as Mijnlieff, but has the benefit of being able to be put out in the open without ridicule.

[Rating: 4/10] Not far enough away from Tic-Tac-Toe for me; playing in the center (especially with a 'pusher' tile, the only kind that prevents your opponent from following up with a center play of their own) is so strong that it seems at first encounter like the whole game is doing that. But that leaves most of the tactical fun of a "decide where your opponent can play" game behind. Play Kulami instead!

[Rating: 4/10] I can't play full abstract games anymore. My brain just starts processing outcomes rather than enjoying the experience.  Albeit this one has some clever rules around what pieces you can play and where, based on the previous players turn. Sadly this means it also delays turns as planning ahead is lessoned (or rather you need to plan for more eventualities).

[Rating: 4.9/10] Fun Tic-Tac-Toe variant, more complex than that, of course. Probably will introduce this to my kids when they're old enough to play it. But it ultimately is Tic-Tac-Toe.

[Rating: 5/10] A little too cramped to be challenging, and I find points scoring a bit of a cop-out in a game like this.  The last 3 or 4 moves were all maiai, i.e. didn't change the score.

[Rating: 5/10] Expanded Tic Tac Toe that actually works. You have 2x4 tiles each (and both players have the same sets of tiles but in their colour) and each of the 4 types of tiles has a special restriction on how the opponent can play his/her next tile when then again places a restriction on how you can place your next tile. It's extremely portable and it's quick so it's a very good travel game.

[Rating: 5/10] Mijnlieff gets into tactical ruts.  I created an expansion to deepen the game, called Mijntrree.  Check the Milnlieff forum to see the expansion set.  So far Mijnlieff is a 5.  But I think Mijntrree is a 6 or 7--time will tell.
